title: Secure Product Development With Mantis

speakers.name: Nick Galloway
speakers.affiliation: Senior Staff Security Developer, Google Cloud

speakers.name: Ruchi Shah
speakers.affiliation: Senior Director, Cloud CISO Security Engineering, Google Cloud

thesis: AI vulnerability scanning is now only the baseline; Google Cloud pairs it with pre-submit scanning, root-cause work (safe-by-construction rewrites, formal verification, extracted specifications) and a spec-driven SDLC in which security engineers become co-architects and code is continuously checked against a written security spec.
summary: Nick Galloway opens by saying AI scanners are table stakes and describes a three-pronged approach: find and patch vulnerabilities, fix root causes, and update the security model across the SDLC. For the first prong he describes Mantis, Google Cloud's internal AI scanner, with planner, researcher, critic and calibrator agents, a find, validate, patch workflow, tuning via per-team threat models, and an open-source blueprint released first as markdown skills and later as an ADK version (with a more efficient and reliable harness) on GitHub. Galloway says deep scans only catch up, so Mantis also runs as a pre-submit check on every change in a few minutes, and Google says it has stopped a big number of bugs before they entered the codebase, though no figure was given. For the second prong he covers rewriting small critical components in memory-safe languages such as Rust, using agents to do the tedious bookkeeping of formal verification on existing code, and using agents to build deterministic extraction code that turns a sprawling real system into an actual specification. That extracted specification is compared with an intended specification built from design docs, RFCs, meeting notes, threat models and comments, and he says mismatches have already revealed surprising bugs. Ruchi Shah then argues the most impactful flaws are design flaws, that point-in-time reviews cannot keep pace with machine-speed development, and shows a spec-driven flow from ideation through rollout with the security bar enforced continuously. Galloway closes with caveats: threat models can suppress real findings, humans dismiss real vulnerabilities as AI slop, extracted specs must be sound, and formal proofs can be tautological.
argument: AI vulnerability scanners are now the baseline, so Google Cloud runs deep periodic scans and also scans every change pre-submit to stop vulnerabilities before they enter the codebase.

Finding bugs is playing catch-up, so root causes should be removed by rewriting critical components in memory-safe languages, using agents for formal verification bookkeeping, and extracting accurate specifications of complex systems.
Comparing an intended specification (from design docs and threat models) with an actual specification extracted from code and configuration surfaces mismatches that humans would miss.
The most impactful vulnerabilities are design flaws, and point-in-time reviews built for human-speed engineering cannot keep up with machine-speed development.
Security should move into the development workflow as living specs and invariants checked continuously, with security engineers acting as co-architects and humans approving intent.

frameworks.name: Three-pronged approach
frameworks.description: One: find and patch vulns (Mantis, deep scans, pre-submit). Two: fix root causes (software rewriting, formal verification, systems understanding, safe coding with security advice in every prompt). Three: update the security model throughout the SDLC.

frameworks.name: Fix root causes in three parts
frameworks.description: Part 1 moving to safe software construction (rewrite in memory-safe languages or prove properties of unsafe code on the side); part 2 understandable systems (specification extraction, intended specification, diff); part 3 a security engineer reviewing every prompt (security requirements inside the coding agent's context or a parallel security agent, a security spec next to the code, humans decide what is acceptable).

frameworks.name: Intended versus extracted specification
frameworks.description: Intended spec is built from design docs, RFCs, meeting notes, human threat models and code comments. Actual spec is extracted by deterministic code, built with agents, from ground truth such as code, configuration and deployment. Disagreements are examined with citations; either the intent is updated or the problem is fixed.

frameworks.name: One spec, carried from ideation to rollout
frameworks.description: Five stages: ideation and design (design docs, RFCs, threat models become the intended side of the spec); obligations (spec checked against the organization's catalogue of security requirements); implementation (coding agents get the spec as context: what must be true, not just what to build); presubmit (checks for changes that weaken security, prototype today); rollout and attestation (humans sign off on what code cannot prove; deviations are fixed or the spec changed on purpose).

frameworks.name: Security bar enforced continuously
frameworks.description: Distributed security requirements are consolidated in one place; an agentic skills approach automates control assessment pre-launch with deterministic measurement post-launch, for full continuous coverage that identifies, remediates and verifies posture violations across production services.

slide_only: Three-pronged approach table: Find and Patch Vulns (Mantis is our AI system for finding vulns in Google Cloud itself; also now deployed as presubmit across the code base, has prevented huge number of bugs so far pre-launch); Fix Root Causes (can AI enable software rewriting, formal verification, systems understanding, and safe coding with security advice in every prompt?); Update Security Model throughout SDLC.

Mantis slide: multiple scanners depending on use case; typical workflow is find, validate, patch; two components to the hard work, infrastructure to run the scanners and LLM integration (prompts, tools, agent hierarchy); tune with threat models.

Open Source slide: a security review toolkit for replicating the workflow, intended as a blueprint or sketch for a shop jig rather than a complete product; skills version as one spec-based distribution method; ADK version for a more efficient and reliable harness; internally the same approach runs across Google Cloud's systems.

Stop the bleeding slide: deep scan the entire Google Cloud codebase but this is playing catch up; scan changes before they merge, with vulnerabilities as review comments on the change; developers or agents do usually act on findings; make agentic patching easily available in tooling developers already use.

Part 1 slide: one path is rewriting key security boundaries and low-level libraries in Rust; another is proving things about unsafe languages on the side, with the key insight that formal verification of memory management properties is just a tremendous amount of tedious bookkeeping.

Part 2 and visualization slides: a dense architecture diagram contrasted with a simplified GCP secure deployment high-level architecture (abstractions and boundaries); both captioned AI generated for illustrative purposes only.
Specification extraction slide: deterministic code does the heavy lifting; agents build and update deterministic inspection and convert specifications into summaries.

Part 3 slide: put security requirements inside the agent's context, not after it, and/or a parallel security agent; a security spec next to the code, updated as the agent works; humans still decide what is acceptable.

Four-box slide on the how-to-build-a-secure-product model: design reviews, implementation reviews, vulnerability research and red teaming, with what would go wrong: code drifts from design, threat models go stale, nobody owns interfaces between systems, point-in-time security reviews lack continuity.

The security review model is antiquated: built for a slower world; machine-speed development overwhelms point-in-time human review; failure modes persist (broken trust boundaries, assumed identities, stale threat models); paradigm shift to co-architects, not gatekeepers, embedding living security specifications into developer and agent workflows.

Embed Security into SDLC via Spec: establish specs as executable contracts (structured Markdown specifications defining security invariants and component contracts before coding); enable early architectural review (security teams as co-architects for critical workstreams); automate security gates with Mantis (presubmit scanning to verify and enforce code against spec invariants).

Where We Go From Here slide: move security engineers from launch reviewers to co-architects; humans write intent, agents convert it into intended spec; machines check code and configuration against intended spec continuously; benefit is fewer late surprises and better coverage.

Caveats slide: human-written threat models may discourage the scanner; humans might dismiss real vulnerabilities (AI slop); low precision with high recall may be desirable (usually not), so measure precision of the system, not of stages; extracted spec must be sound with a deterministic oracle for reachability questions being gold; beware conflicting or vague security requirements; beware tautologies (proving 2 == 2).
Thanks slide names Nick Galloway, Senior Staff Security Developer, and Ruchi Shah, Sr. Director, Cloud CISO Security Engineering, with LinkedIn profiles and thanks to Mantis contributors.

offense: A scanner given a threat model that says a component runs in a sandbox can dismiss a real sandbox escape as impossible, so a stale or over-trusting threat model suppresses real findings.

Failure modes the speakers see in product security: code drifts from design, threat models go stale, nobody owns interfaces between systems, point-in-time reviews lack continuity, and attackers move at machine speed.
defense: Scan every change pre-submit within a few minutes and post findings as review comments before the code merges; put agentic patching in tools developers already use, ahead of the pull request if possible.
Tune scanners per team with threat-model modifications to the rubric, but check that threat models do not suppress real findings.
Rewrite small, critical components (boot loaders, kernel drivers, security boundaries, low-level libraries) in memory-safe languages, or use agents to formally verify existing unsafe code.
Have agents build deterministic code that extracts a system's actual specification, then diff it against an intended specification derived from design docs, RFCs and threat models.

Put security requirements inside the coding agent's context or run a parallel security agent, require agents to state assumptions, and keep a security spec next to the code, updated as the agent works.
Consolidate all security requirements in one place (the security bar), automate control assessments with skills, and measure post-launch deterministically.
Treat specs as executable contracts with security invariants, review specs separately from derived code, and gate merges on spec invariants; generate specs for brownfield code by reverse engineering.
Prefer static or deterministic checks where possible and use AI only where non-determinism is needed.
Measure precision of the whole system rather than of stages, and watch for tautological proofs when using SMT or Lean.
takeaways: As a practice to test, treat AI scanning as baseline and move it to pre-submit with a latency budget of a few minutes, so vulnerabilities are review comments rather than tickets.

As a practice to test, build a security spec per product that records intended invariants, extract an actual spec from code and configuration, and review mismatches continuously instead of at launch gates.

On one reported incident, re-audit your scanner's inputs, since threat models and prior human decisions can teach the scanner to ignore real issues, and feed human dismissal of findings as slop back as ground truth for tuning.
As a direction to test, reposition product security engineers as co-architects embedded early, with agents carrying the security bar into the developer's context.
When using formal methods with AI, check that proofs are not tautological and that extracted specs are sound before relying on them.
limits: Speaker had no number to share for how many bugs pre-submit scanning has stopped.
Mantis is not bug free and the open source version is a blueprint rather than a complete product.
Formal verification and rewriting results are described as promising but not detailed.
Extracted specifications may lose some information, and they must be mostly deterministic and sound.
Internal specification tooling is custom to Google and may not be open sourced.
Pre-submit checks for spec weakening are a prototype today.
critique: The talk is largely a description of an internal approach with almost no quantitative evidence: no bug counts, no false positive rates, no latency distributions, no comparison of agent architectures, so the claims about effectiveness rest on assertion.
The specification extraction and diff approach was validated only by informal human sampling, and the diagrams shown were labeled AI generated for illustrative purposes.
The talk gave no data on the cost of keeping specs accurate or on ownership across teams.
Mantis was built by the speakers' company, Google Cloud.
The internal tooling for the second and third prongs is not available.
The talk advises tuning scanners with threat models and also describes a threat model suppressing a real finding; it was a single incident and no data on the tradeoff was given.
qa: Question on whether the generated system diagram came from Mantis and whether it is cloud agnostic: the two diagrams shown were AI-generated illustrations; the internal tooling is not open source and is custom to Google, and whether it lands in Mantis OSS is unknown.

Question on incorporating security misconfiguration or standards into Mantis and generating threat models from them: Galloway said probably, but use AI only where non-determinism is needed, because anything checkable statically is faster and does not need complex harnesses and evals.

Question from the moderator on whether the system works at very high velocity if code moves away from the Git model (referring to an Anthropic revision-system change the questioner called Scion): Galloway said it will work better because agents are ready to review everything, and they aim to move even earlier than pre-submit, such as in Code Mender in Anti-Gravity before a pull request is sent.

key_frames.caption: Mantis architecture summary: multiple scanners, find, validate, patch workflow, infrastructure plus LLM integration, tuned with threat models.
One Spec, Carried From Ideation to Rollout: the five-stage spec-driven flow from design docs through obligations, implementation, presubmit and attestation.
Caveats slide: threat models that discourage the scanner, human dismissal as AI slop, precision of the system, sound extracted specs and tautological proofs.
Part 1 slide on safe software construction: rewrite in memory-safe languages or use AI for tedious formal-verification bookkeeping.
Part 3 slide: put security requirements in the coding agent's context, keep a living security spec, and keep humans deciding what is acceptable.

signal.reason: The talk presents an architecture for specification-driven product security with listed caveats; no measured results were shown and much of the tooling is internal.

caveats: The captions say 'Code Mentor in Anti-Gravity'; no slide shows the product name, and this record gives it as Code Mender, an unconfirmed reading.
The final shot is a camera view of the Q&A with no slide.
The video description says Galloway's affiliation is 'AI for security and security for AI, Google Cloud'; the slide says Senior Staff Security Developer, and this record uses the slide.
